question.title: BigQuery ML
question.scenario: A marketing team wants to predict customer churn using historical data stored in BigQuery but lacks machine learning expertise.
question.question-text: Which BigQuery feature enables creating and training machine learning models using SQL?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the BigQuery feature that lets SQL users build, train, and run machine learning models without leaving the BigQuery environment or learning Python.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: BigQuery ML enables users to create, train, and execute machine learning models using standard SQL queries directly within BigQuery. It removes the need to export data or learn a separate ML framework. Vertex AI (B) is the full-featured ML platform requiring Python SDK knowledge. AI Platform (C) is the predecessor to Vertex AI. AutoML Tables (D) is now part of Vertex AI and requires a different workflow with a dedicated UI, not SQL statements.

ul.li: The CREATE MODEL statement trains models on BigQuery data, supporting logistic regression, k-means clustering, matrix factorization, time-series ARIMA, boosted trees, and deep neural networks.
ML.PREDICT applies a trained model to new data for inference, and ML.EVALUATE returns accuracy metrics like precision, recall, and AUC so analysts can assess model quality in SQL.
BigQuery ML can import pre-trained TensorFlow and ONNX models, and export trained BQML models to Vertex AI for serving behind a low-latency prediction endpoint.
Feature preprocessing functions like ML.BUCKETIZE, ML.FEATURE_CROSS, and ML.POLYNOMIAL_EXPAND let analysts engineer features directly in the CREATE MODEL statement without separate ETL.

question.title: Cloud Trace
question.scenario: A microservices application is experiencing latency issues, and the team needs to identify which service in the request chain is causing delays.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides distributed tracing to analyze request latency across services?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The service you need collects latency data as requests flow through multiple services and visualizes the timing breakdown in a waterfall trace view.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Trace collects latency data from applications and displays it in a waterfall trace view showing time spent in each service for a given request. It helps pinpoint bottlenecks in distributed systems and integrates with OpenTelemetry for portable instrumentation. Cloud Profiler (A) profiles CPU and memory usage at the function level within a single service. Cloud Monitoring (B) tracks aggregate metrics but does not trace individual requests. Cloud Debugger (C) inspects application state at specific code locations without stopping execution.

ul.li: Trace context propagates through standard HTTP headers (W3C Trace Context or X-Cloud-Trace-Context) across service boundaries, linking spans from different services into a single end-to-end trace.

Analysis reports show latency distributions, percentile breakdowns (p50, p95, p99), and trends over time, helping teams identify whether latency regressions are gradual or tied to specific deployments.
OpenTelemetry SDK provides vendor-neutral instrumentation for traces, so applications instrumented with OpenTelemetry can export to Cloud Trace, Jaeger, or Zipkin without code changes.
Cloud Trace automatically correlates with Cloud Logging entries, so clicking a trace span links directly to the log entries emitted during that span's execution window.

question.title: Cloud Scheduler
question.scenario: An application needs to trigger a Cloud Function every hour to check for and process new files in a Cloud Storage bucket.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides fully managed cron job scheduling?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The service you need is a managed cron scheduler that triggers HTTP endpoints, Pub/Sub topics, or App Engine handlers on a user-defined schedule using unix-cron syntax.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Scheduler is a fully managed cron job service that triggers targets on a schedule defined using unix-cron syntax. It supports HTTP/S endpoints, Pub/Sub topics, and App Engine applications as targets. Cloud Tasks (A) manages task queues for asynchronous dispatch but does not provide cron scheduling. Cloud Composer (B) orchestrates complex data pipelines with Airflow, which is heavy for a simple hourly trigger. Cloud Workflows (C) orchestrates multi-step processes but is not a cron scheduler itself.

ul.li: Cloud Scheduler supports OIDC and OAuth tokens for authenticated HTTP requests, enabling secure triggering of Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, and other identity-aware endpoints without exposing public URLs.
Retry configuration allows specifying maximum retry attempts, minimum and maximum backoff intervals, and retry duration, handling transient failures gracefully without manual intervention.
Time zones can be specified per job using IANA time zone identifiers (e.g., America/Los_Angeles), ensuring schedules align with business hours regardless of the GCP region hosting the job.
Cloud Scheduler is commonly paired with Pub/Sub to decouple the schedule from the handler: the scheduler publishes a message on schedule, and any number of subscribers can react independently.

question.title: Dataflow Streaming Exactly-Once
question.scenario: A financial services company processes real-time transactions with Dataflow and requires exactly-once processing to ensure no transactions are processed twice or lost.
question.question-text: Which Dataflow feature guarantees that each record is processed exactly once in streaming pipelines?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Dataflow's Streaming Engine combines checkpointing, state management, and record deduplication to guarantee each record is processed exactly once even when workers fail.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Dataflow provides exactly-once processing semantics in streaming pipelines through a combination of checkpointing, persistent state management, and record-level deduplication. Even when workers fail and restart, each record is guaranteed to be processed exactly once. Watermarks (A) track event-time progress for windowing but do not provide delivery guarantees. At-least-once (B) guarantees delivery but allows duplicates. Dead letter queues (D) handle failed messages but do not ensure processing exactly once.

ul.li: Checkpoints persist intermediate processing state to durable storage at regular intervals, enabling the system to resume from the last consistent state after a worker failure without reprocessing already-committed records.

Record IDs assigned by the source (e.g., Pub/Sub message IDs) enable deduplication: if a record is replayed after a failure, the system recognizes the duplicate and discards it before applying transforms.
Exactly-once semantics extend end-to-end to supported sinks like BigQuery (using buffered writes) and Cloud Storage, so the guarantee covers the full pipeline from ingestion through output.
Streaming Engine mode offloads shuffle and state storage from worker VMs to a Google-managed backend, improving checkpoint reliability and reducing the blast radius of individual worker failures.

question.title: Dataproc Metastore
question.scenario: Multiple Dataproc clusters and Dataflow jobs need to share a common Hive metastore for consistent table definitions without managing a separate metastore service.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides a fully managed Hive metastore?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google Cloud offers a fully managed, highly available Hive metastore service that multiple Dataproc clusters and other big data tools can share as a central metadata repository.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Dataproc Metastore is a fully managed, highly available Hive metastore that serves as a central metadata repository shared across Dataproc clusters, Dataflow pipelines, and other big data services. Data Catalog (A) provides metadata discovery and governance but is not a Hive-compatible metastore. Cloud SQL (B) could host a metastore database manually, but managing the schema, availability, and compatibility is your responsibility. BigQuery (D) has its own metadata system and is not a Hive metastore.

ul.li: Dataproc Metastore supports Apache Hive Metastore protocol and AWS Glue-compatible mode, enabling migration from on-premises Hive environments or AWS-based data lakes with minimal schema changes.
Integration with Data Catalog provides unified metadata search and discovery, so table definitions stored in the Hive metastore are automatically visible in Data Catalog's search and lineage views.

Managed metastore instances eliminate the per-cluster metastore startup penalty, since ephemeral Dataproc clusters can connect to the persistent metastore immediately on creation rather than initializing their own.
Scheduled backups and point-in-time restore protect metastore data, and multi-region configurations provide high availability, ensuring that metadata is not lost even during regional outages.

question.title: Service Mesh Observability
question.scenario: A microservices application running on GKE needs automatic mTLS, traffic management, and observability without modifying application code.
question.question-text: Which GKE feature provides service mesh capabilities with built-in observability?

choices.choice: Anthos Service Mesh (or Cloud Service Mesh)

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The GKE feature you need provides a managed Istio-based service mesh that handles mTLS encryption, traffic routing, and telemetry collection via sidecar proxies without application code changes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Anthos Service Mesh (also called Cloud Service Mesh) is a managed Istio-based service mesh that provides mutual TLS encryption, traffic management, and observability for microservices on GKE. It automatically collects telemetry and provides topology dashboards without code modifications. GKE Ingress (B) manages external HTTP/S traffic routing to services but does not provide service-to-service encryption, traffic splitting, or mesh-level observability. Cloud Load Balancing (C) distributes traffic at the infrastructure level. Cloud Armor (D) provides WAF and DDoS protection for external endpoints.

ul.li: Envoy sidecar proxies are injected alongside each application container and handle all inbound and outbound traffic transparently, providing mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, and telemetry without any application code changes.
Service-level SLOs can be defined and monitored directly in the Cloud Service Mesh dashboard, showing error rates, latency percentiles, and availability against configured targets for each service.

Traffic splitting enables canary deployments and A/B testing at the mesh level by routing a configurable percentage of requests to different service versions based on HTTP headers, weights, or other criteria.

The service topology graph provides a real-time visualization of service dependencies, request rates, error rates, and latency between services, making it easy to identify the blast radius of a failing service.
